orders.trial_court_action: Granted the owner’s and tenants’ separate motions for summary judgment dismissing the claims against them.

facts.factual_summary: A real estate agent visiting for prospective renters allegedly slipped while descending interior stairs. She believed she stepped on a shoe, but had not seen it on the top step. The staircase lacked a handrail, and she described reaching for support as she lost her balance.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the duty of an owner or tenant in possession to maintain reasonably safe premises. Defendants did not establish entitlement to dismissal on the missing-handrail theory.

Attributing the fall to a shoe required speculation. The plaintiff’s testimony about reaching for support nevertheless raised a triable question whether the absence of a handrail contributed to her injury.
Defendants’ initial showing was insufficient, so the court did not assess the opposition papers. It declined to consider a contention the tenants raised for the first time on appeal.

evidence_discussed.description: The agent described the shoes, obstructed view and attempt to regain balance. The tenants and owner described what they had and had not seen on the stairs.

quality.notes: One order resolved two separate motions. The court reversed both dismissals despite agreeing that causation by a shoe was speculative.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Colabella, J.), entered January 4, 2010, which granted the motion of the defendant Benjamin Ramirez and the separate motion of the defendants Julie C. Magee and Timothy M. Magee, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with one bill of *1266 costs payable by the defendants appearing separately and filing separate briefs, and the defendants’ separate motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them are denied.

On May 20, 2008 the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while attempting to walk down an interior staircase within a residence owned by the defendant Benjamin Ramirez, part of which Ramirez rented to the defendants Julie C. Magee and Timothy M. Magee (hereinafter together the Magees).

The staircase led from the kitchen within the portion of the home rented by the Magees, to a foyer for the back entrance to the home and the door to the basement apartment, which was utilized by Ramirez.

Upon arriving at the residence, the plaintiff, a real estate agent who was there to preview the residence for clients interested in renting it, gained entry to the home through the use of a lock box at the rear entrance and climbed the subject staircase.
On her way up the staircase to the kitchen, she noticed shoes on various steps. The plaintiff did not recall shoes being on the top step. It is undisputed that the subject staircase had no handrail.

When walking down that same staircase following Mrs. Magee on their way down to the basement apartment, the plaintiff allegedly slipped when she stepped on something which she believed to be a shoe situated on the top step, which caused her to fall down the remaining four or five steps.
Although the plaintiff did not see a shoe on the top step as she stepped down, she testified at her deposition that she could not see the top step because the kitchen door opened over the staircase.

She also stated that as she reached out to balance herself, she hit the door, “which came back at [her].” As she “tried to grab onto something, there was nothing to grab onto,” and her right ankle rolled, causing her to lose her balance and fall down the staircase.

Prior to the accident, which allegedly occurred at approximately 1:30 p.m., Mrs. Magee had used the subject staircase on two occasions, at approximately 8:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m., and on those two occasions she did not observe shoes on the steps.

Both of the Magees testified that their family would remove their shoes and leave them on the tiled floor of the back entrance foyer; however, on occasion, both had observed shoes on the steps. Ramirez testified at his deposition that he never observed any shoes on the subject staircase.
We agree with the plaintiff that the Supreme Court improperly granted the motions.
An owner or tenant in possession of realty owes a duty to maintain the property in a reasonably safe condition”
the Supreme Court properly determined that a jury would be required to speculate that the shoe caused the plaintiffs fall
However, with respect to the absence of a handrail for the subject staircase, the defendants failed to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law
a triable issue of fact exists as to whether the absence of the handrail was a proximate cause of the plaintiffs injury
Accordingly, the Supreme Court erred in granting the motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
we do not need to reach the question of the sufficiency of the plaintiffs opposition papers
The Magees’ remaining contention is not properly before this Court, as it is raised for the first time on appeal.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted the shopping center owner’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Baez alleged that her foot came into contact with a hole while she walked through the parking lot of defendant’s shopping center, causing her to trip and fall.

legal_issues.finding: The court included creation in the owner’s initial burden. Its decision turned on the failure to negate constructive notice.
Actual notice was part of the stated standard. The court made no separate finding of actual notice.
The manager described routine inspections but supplied no evidence of a specific inspection before Baez fell. The owner failed to establish lack of constructive notice.
Failure to meet the initial burden required denial regardless of the sufficiency of the opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: The property manager’s deposition and affidavit addressed general inspection practices but did not identify a last inspection of the accident site.

quality.notes: Reversal denied the defense motion. The court did not find that the owner actually knew about the hole.

evidence.quote: Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Roy S. Mahon, J.), entered June 16, 2016. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

The plaintiff Maria De Los Angeles Baez (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly was walking in the parking lot of a shopping center owned by the defendant when her foot came into contact with a hole in the parking lot, causing her to trip and fall.
The Supreme Court granted the motion, and the plaintiffs appeal.

A defendant who moves for summary judgment in a trip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it did not create the hazardous condition which allegedly caused the fall, and did not have actual or constructive notice of that condition for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it
In support of its motion, the defendant failed to demonstrate that it lacked constructive notice of the hazardous condition which allegedly caused the injured plaintiff's fall.

The defendant relied upon, inter alia, the deposition testimony and affidavit of the property manager, which merely referred to her general inspection practices for the parking lot and provided no evidence regarding any specific inspection of the area in question prior to the injured plaintiff's fall

The defendant's failure to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law required the denial of its motion, regardless of the sufficiency of the plaintiffs' papers in opposition
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.trial_court_action: Denied Court Restoration’s motion to dismiss the amended complaint and all cross claims against it on summary judgment.

facts.factual_summary: Maldonado allegedly tripped on a depressed drain near the front door of her parents’ condominium complex. A planter that ordinarily blocked access to the drain had been removed during construction.

legal_issues.finding: The contractor’s submissions did not establish that the drain was trivial under the surrounding circumstances. Its dimensions alone could not decide actionability.
Because the contractor failed to meet its initial burden, the court did not reach the sufficiency of the opposition or its remaining contention.

evidence_discussed.description: The condominium superintendent’s deposition was also before the court.
Maldonado took the submitted photograph of the drain on the accident date.

quality.notes: The drain was near the private complex’s entrance where a planter ordinarily restricted access. The contractor’s motion reached the direct injury claim as well as cross claims. Shared calibration overlap: CAL_002.

evidence.quote: Dana Maldonado, Respondent, v 2121 Shore Condominium et al., Defendants, and Court Restoration, Inc., Appellant.

the defendant Court Restoration, Inc., appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Ash, J.), dated December 3, 2014, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint and all cross claims insofar as asserted against it.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell in front of her parents' condominium complex on a depressed drain near the front door entrance.
A large planter, which usually blocked access to the area in which the drain was situated, had been removed due to ongoing construction.
which was performing the construction at the subject condominium complex at the time of the accident.

The appellant moved for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint and all cross claims insofar as asserted against it, contending that the alleged defect was not actionable because it was trivial.
We affirm.

In determining whether a defect is trivial, the court must examine all of the facts presented, including the "width, depth, elevation, irregularity and appearance of the defect along with the time, place and circumstance of the injury"
a holding of triviality [is] to be based on all the specific facts and circumstances of the case, not size alone"

the evidence submitted by the appellant, including transcripts of the deposition testimony of the plaintiff and the condominium complex's superintendent, and a photograph of the subject drain taken by the plaintiff on the date of the accident, was insufficient to establish, prima facie, that, given the circumstances surrounding this accident, the defect was trivial as a matter of law and, thus, not actionable

In light of our determination, we need not address the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposing papers ( see Winegrad v New York Univ. Med. Ctr. , 64 NY2d 851, 853 [1985]) or the appellant's remaining contention.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the appellant's motion for summary judgment.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Pusey, a home healthcare aide who had worked at the premises for almost a year, was trying to reenter the house after being locked out. At about 8 p.m., she tripped on a stake and wire supporting a bush in the flower bed.

legal_issues.finding: The flower bed was not intended for passage. The homeowners could not reasonably foresee Pusey crossing it, and had no duty to warn of or protect against the unlit stake and wire there.

evidence_discussed.description: The parties’ depositions supported the conclusion that the area was not intended for use as a path.

quality.notes: The court decided foreseeability based on the location and use of the flower bed. The plaintiff’s job is explicit; her employer is not identified.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Martha L. Luft, J.), dated July 6, 2017. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On October 18, 2013, at approximately 8:00 p.m., the plaintiff, a home healthcare aide, tripped and fell on a stake and wire supporting a bush in a dirt flower bed immediately adjacent to the front of the defendants' house.

At the time of the accident, the plaintiff, who had been working at the defendants' premises for almost a year, was trying to regain entry to the house after being accidentally locked out of the house.
Property owners and occupiers owe a duty of reasonable care under the circumstances to keep their premises safe

The defendants established, prima facie, that given the position of the stake and wire in the dirt flower bed immediately adjacent to the front of the defendants' home, the failure to illuminate the stake and wire did not pose a reasonably foreseeable hazard
The defendants were under no duty to warn of or otherwise protect the plaintiff from a condition that posed no reasonably foreseeable hazard
Here, it was not foreseeable that the plaintiff would traverse the area where she fell.

The evidence submitted in support of the defendants' motion, which included the deposition testimony of the parties, [*2] established that this area of the premises was not intended to be used as a path or thoroughfare.
In opposition to the defendants' prima facie showing, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to grant the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Suffolk County order dated October 17, 2022, in consolidated actions
orders.trial_court_action: Granted Steel’s and Broadway’s separate motions dismissing the complaint as against each defendant.

facts.factual_summary: Walsh allegedly slipped on ice in the exterior loading bay of the trucking terminal where he worked. Steel owned the terminal and leased it to his employer, which hired Broadway for snow and ice removal.

legal_issues.finding: Steel did not retain the control or lease obligation needed to impose a snow-removal duty. Broadway’s service contract did not establish a duty to Walsh on this record.
Steel showed prima facie that it did not create the ice. Walsh also failed to raise a triable issue that Broadway launched an instrument of harm.
Steel made a prima facie showing that it lacked actual notice of the ice.
Steel made a prima facie showing that it lacked constructive notice of the ice.
Steel showed that it was out of possession, had no snow-removal obligation under the lease, and retained insufficient control for liability.
Walsh was not a party to the snow-removal contract. The pleadings did not invoke facts supporting any Espinal exception, and the opposition raised no triable issue under those exceptions.
Because the pleadings did not allege facts supporting an Espinal exception, Broadway did not have to affirmatively negate the exceptions to make its initial showing.

evidence_discussed.description: The court considered Steel’s responsibilities under its lease and Walsh’s status in relation to the snow-removal contract.

quality.notes: Two actions and two defense motions were resolved by one appealed order. Both dismissals were affirmed.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (John H. Rouse, J.), dated October 17, 2022. The order granted the defendants' separate motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with one bill of costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on ice on the floor of the exterior loading bay at the trucking terminal where he worked.
The subject premises were owned by the defendant Steel O-III, LLC (hereinafter Steel), and were leased to the plaintiff's employer, Old Dominion Freight Lines, Inc. (hereinafter Old Dominion).

Thereafter, the plaintiff commenced this action against Steel and a separate action against the defendant Broadway Maintenance, LLC (hereinafter Broadway), the company hired by Old Dominion to perform snow and ice removal services at the premises. The two actions were later consolidated.
The Supreme Court properly granted Steel's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

Here, Steel established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting evidence that it was an out-of-possession landlord who was not obligated under the lease to remove snow and ice from the premises and did not retain a sufficient degree of control over the premises to provide a basis for liability
Moreover, Steel established, prima facie, that it did not create the alleged icy condition and that it did not have actual or constructive notice of the icy condition
The Supreme Court also properly granted Broadway's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

However, a party that enters into a contract to render services may be said to have assumed a duty of care, and thus, be potentially liable in tort to third persons, where (1) the contracting party, in failing to exercise reasonable care in the performance of its duties, launches a force or instrument of harm, (2) the plaintiff detrimentally relies on the continued performance of the contracting party's duties, or (3) the contracting party has entirely displaced the other party's duty to maintain the premises safely"

Here, Broadway demonstrated its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it by coming forward with evidence that the plaintiff was not a party to the snow removal contract

Since the plaintiff did not allege facts in the pleadings that would establish the possible applicability of any of the Espinal exceptions, Broadway was not required to affirmatively demonstrate that these exceptions did not apply in order to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law

In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether Broadway launched an instrument of harm ( see Bronstein v Benderson Dev. Co., LLC , 167 AD3d 837 , 839 [2018]; Reisert v Mayne Constr. of Long Is., Inc. , 165 AD3d at 856) and failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to the applicability of the other Espinal exceptions.
The plaintiff's remaining contentions either are without merit or not properly before this Court.
